title: SYSK’s Summer Movie Playlist: Special Effects: A Short History
summary: Summer movie playlist episode on the history of movie special effects. The hosts divide effects into practical (in front of the camera), in-camera (done inside the camera, such as slow motion, stop trick, double exposure), and post-production (CGI and digital compositing). They trace early trickery from still photography and Alfred Clark's stop trick in The Execution of Mary, Queen of Scots, to Georges Méliès and A Trip to the Moon, matte painting (including Norman Dunn's original negative matte painting), rear and front projection, the shake-the-car technique, green screen and the Williams process in The Invisible Man, optical printers, motion control cameras (Dykstraflex on Star Wars), and Jurassic Park's mixed techniques. They cover pioneers such as Lon Chaney, Willis O'Brien, Ray Harryhausen, Millicent Patrick, Dick Smith, Rick Baker, Stan Winston, and Tom Savini, the companies ILM and WETA, motion capture, and early CGI firsts such as Young Sherlock Holmes, Looker, and Star Trek II: The Wrath of Khan. They close with de-aging, deepfakes, and a return to practical effects. The episode ends with a listener email about solar panels and roof age.

segments.title: Opening and playlist intro
segments.summary: Josh introduces the playlist episode on special effects, followed by banter about hats, lawnmowers, and movies.

segments.title: Off-topic banter
segments.summary: Hosts chat about hats, battery lawnmowers, and movies such as Sky Captain and The Changeling before getting back to the topic.
topics: Sky Captain and the World of Tomorrow

segments.title: Three categories of special effects
segments.summary: Effects are divided into practical (in front of the camera, such as makeup, prosthetics, explosions, squibs, and fire), in-camera (done inside the camera, such as slow motion and fast motion), and post-production effects, which are mostly CGI today.

segments.title: In-camera tricks and stop motion
segments.summary: Discussion of in-camera techniques such as slow motion, fast motion, substitution tricks like Bewitched, craft service, and stop motion animation.

segments.title: Post-production CGI and early still-photo tricks
segments.summary: Computers now do work that once took months. Early filmmakers built on still-photography tricks such as double exposure.

segments.title: Early pioneers: Alfred Clark and Georges Méliès
segments.summary: Alfred Clark's stop trick in The Execution of Mary, Queen of Scots is described, along with how a camera jam in Paris led Méliès to the stop trick. Méliès is called the father of special effects, and his 1902 A Trip to the Moon is discussed.

segments.title: Ad break
segments.summary: Break before the matte painting segment.

segments.title: Matte painting and original negative matte painting
segments.summary: Matte painting is explained as painting on glass placed in front of a camera to extend sets, with examples such as Escape from New York, Mary Poppins, and Superman. Norman Dunn's original negative matte painting technique is described, along with the related rear and front projection methods.

segments.title: Car driving scenes and shaking the car
segments.summary: Describes how fake driving scenes are staged, with actors in a still car while crew shake it and use lights and fake rain. Pulp Fiction's rear projection is mentioned.

segments.title: Green screen, blue screen, and the Williams process
segments.summary: Early green screen with sodium vapor lights, and the Williams process used in The Invisible Man, where a black bodysuit and black background left nothing exposed on film. The optical printer is introduced, and the switch from blue to green screen is discussed.

segments.title: Optical printer compositing
segments.summary: The optical printer is explained as a projector and camera working together to combine multiple film elements into one shot.

segments.title: Motion control cameras
segments.summary: Motion control cameras are explained as machines that move cameras precisely and repeatably, often used for commercials and food shoots.

segments.title: Star Wars models and Jurassic Park
segments.summary: Star Wars used motion control cameras on still models, using the Dykstraflex system from John Dykstra and optical printing to make the ships appear to move. Jurassic Park's raptor kitchen scene mixed puppets, costumed actors, animatronics, and CGI. The Abyss is discussed as an early Oscar-winning CGI effect.

segments.title: Ed Harris and off-topic banter
segments.summary: Brief tangent about Ed Harris, followed by a break.

segments.title: Wire removal and the Dykstraflex legacy
segments.summary: Wire removal is discussed with examples from Mad Max and Forrest Gump. Hosts discuss the excess of digital effects and whether practical effects will return.

segments.title: Legendary makeup and effects artists
segments.summary: Lon Chaney as the Man of a Thousand Faces, Willis O'Brien's stop motion work on King Kong (1933), which took about seven weeks to film the fight, and Ray Harryhausen's work on Jason and the Argonauts and Clash of the Titans are covered.

segments.title: Millicent Patrick, Dick Smith, and other makeup artists
segments.summary: Millicent Patrick's uncredited work on the Gill Man mask for Creature from the Black Lagoon is discussed. Dick Smith's aging makeup on Marlon Brando and Dustin Hoffman is covered.

segments.title: Rick Baker, Stan Winston, and Tom Savini
segments.summary: Rick Baker and Stan Winston are described as trailblazers. Their credits include An American Werewolf in London, Star Wars Mos Eisley Cantina, Predator, and Terminator. Stan Winston's Friday the 13th Part 2 and Tom Savini are also covered.

segments.title: ILM, WETA, and motion capture
segments.summary: ILM was founded for Lucas and WETA is Peter Jackson's company. Motion capture is explained, and Gollum from Lord of the Rings is mentioned as an early full CGI character.

segments.title: First CGI firsts
segments.summary: Young Sherlock Holmes (1985) is named as the first full CGI character, while Looker is noted for the first digital composite of a full-screen live-action image. Early CGI computer screens are also covered.

segments.title: Wrath of Khan CGI, de-aging, and deepfakes
segments.summary: The Genesis sequence in Star Trek II: The Wrath of Khan is named as an early full CGI scene, and Tron's animation is mentioned. De-aging in The Irishman and Gemini Man is discussed, along with deepfakes.

segments.title: Color grading and closing thoughts
segments.summary: Digital color grading is compared with older optical methods, using O Brother, Where Art Thou? as an example. The hosts wrap up the topic.

segments.title: Listener mail on solar panels and roofs
segments.summary: A listener writes in to say that roof age should be considered before installing solar panels, since reroofing with panels installed is costly. The Matrix anniversary and John Wick are also briefly mentioned.

segments.title: Listener email sign-off
segments.summary: The hosts thank the listener and recommend his roofing business.

segments.title: Outro
segments.summary: Hosts give contact information and sign off.
